questions.stem: A patient with liver cirrhosis has blood tests showing elevated ammonia levels and low urea levels. Which liver function has been impaired?

options.text: Bile production for fat digestion
Deamination of excess amino acids and conversion of ammonia to urea
Storage of glycogen from excess glucose
Production of red blood cells

questions.explanation: The liver deaminates excess amino acids, removing the amino group which forms toxic ammonia. Normally, the liver quickly converts ammonia to less toxic urea via the ornithine cycle. In liver disease, this process fails, so ammonia builds up and urea production falls.

questions.stem: After eating a large carbohydrate-rich meal, blood glucose rises. How does the liver help to regulate blood glucose in this situation?

options.text: The liver excretes excess glucose in bile
The liver converts excess glucose to glycogen for storage, stimulated by insulin
The liver converts glucose directly into urea
The liver sends glucose to the kidneys for excretion

questions.explanation: When blood glucose is high, the pancreas releases insulin, which stimulates liver cells to convert excess glucose into glycogen (glycogenesis) for storage. This brings blood glucose levels back to normal. The liver can also convert excess glucose into lipids.

questions.stem: A person consumes a high-protein diet. What happens to the excess amino acids that the body cannot store?

options.text: They are stored as protein reserves in the muscles
They are excreted whole by the kidneys
They are deaminated in the liver; the amino group becomes urea and the remainder is used for respiration
They are converted to fat and stored without any waste products

questions.explanation: The body cannot store excess amino acids. In the liver, deamination removes the amino group (NH₂), which is converted to ammonia and then to urea for excretion by the kidneys. The remaining carbon-containing keto acid can be respired for energy or converted to fat or glucose.

questions.stem: The liver receives blood from two sources: the hepatic artery and the hepatic portal vein. Why does the liver need this dual blood supply?

options.text: The hepatic artery delivers nutrients; the hepatic portal vein delivers oxygen
The hepatic artery delivers oxygenated blood for liver cell respiration; the hepatic portal vein brings nutrient-rich blood from the gut for processing
Both vessels deliver identical blood; the dual supply is a backup
The hepatic portal vein removes waste; the hepatic artery adds nutrients

questions.explanation: The hepatic artery supplies oxygenated blood from the heart for the liver's own metabolic needs. The hepatic portal vein carries blood rich in absorbed nutrients (and potentially toxins) directly from the digestive system, allowing the liver to process, store, or detoxify these substances.

questions.stem: A patient who has been drinking alcohol heavily for many years develops liver damage. Why is the liver particularly affected by chronic alcohol consumption?

options.text: Alcohol is stored in the liver as glycogen
The liver is responsible for detoxifying alcohol, and prolonged exposure damages liver cells, leading to cirrhosis
Alcohol prevents the liver from producing bile
Alcohol increases blood flow to the liver, causing it to swell

questions.explanation: The liver detoxifies harmful substances including alcohol. Liver cells break down alcohol using enzymes, but chronic heavy drinking overwhelms this process and produces toxic by-products that damage and destroy liver cells. Over time, scar tissue replaces functional liver tissue (cirrhosis).
